evidence.title: Audited large language model triage for systematic review screening in national clinical guideline production: validation and prospective deployment
evidence.outcome: False negatives found by audit of random sample of AI-excluded records
evidence.effect: Among 600 randomly sampled AI-excluded records, none was confirmed as a final false negative. In the 680-record audit, all 38 final retained records had been AI flagged.
evidence.quote: Across 600 randomly sampled AI-excluded records from the migraine and dementia programmes, none was confirmed as a final false negative after post-unblinding adjudication; across the completed 680-record audit, all 38 final retained records had been AI flagged, whereas locked blinded human consensus missed seven.

commentary.bottom_line: One Swedish deployment study audited random samples of AI-excluded records and found no confirmed false negatives among 600 records, which suggests that sample-based spot-checks can be run at scale and can document AI error rates. No study tested whether periodic spot-checking detects errors that accumulate over time or improves reporting accuracy, so the evidence for the practice as written remains thin.

perspectives.view: A single prospective study with a comparator (n=74,679 records) tested a random-sample audit. Its design starts at low certainty. It measured errors at one point rather than monitoring over time, which makes it indirect. Zero events in 600 records gives an imprecise estimate. These limits lead to a very low rating.

In the 600-record audit, no AI-excluded record was confirmed as a final false negative, and all 38 retained records in the 680-record audit had been AI flagged. By the rule of three, a zero count in 600 is still compatible with a miss rate near 0.5%. Detection of rare errors would therefore require larger or repeated samples.

The study embedded random-sample audits in a live deployment, which suggests that spot-checks can run alongside AI-assisted record handling. The report does not describe how often audits recurred, who performed them, or how data completeness was tracked. Fidelity over time therefore remains untested.

Audits of 600 and 680 records against a pool of 74,679 represent a small fraction of volume. This suggests that sample-based checking may cost far less than full manual review. The study did not report staff hours or cost per audit, so budgeting would have to rely on local estimates.

The only test took place in Sweden, and the summary gives no breakdown by insurance, language, or literacy. Error rates in a pooled random sample can mask higher error rates in small subgroups. Health systems may need to stratify their samples to see errors concentrated in underserved patients.

commentary.research_gap: No study has measured whether periodic spot-checks and ongoing error-rate and completeness monitoring detect drift or accumulating errors after deployment, particularly in quality reporting. The field also lacks data on the sample sizes and audit frequency needed to detect low error rates, and on the staff time and cost of sustained auditing.
commentary.underserved_note: The single test was conducted in Sweden and reported no data on Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Whether random audits capture errors that fall disproportionately on these groups is unknown, and pooled audit results should not be assumed to apply to them.
